blocks.text: Cover batching, retry policies, conflict reduction, and privacy.

Begin with confirmed per-key values, optimistic overlays, and a durable command queue. Measure queue age, per-key conflict rate, convergence, and rejected intent before tuning batching, retry, or tab coordination.

Preference sync quality checks:
- Batching preserves command identity and each key's base revision.
- Retry uses backoff and stops on policy-relevant conflicts.
- Independent keys converge without silently overwriting the same key.
- Privacy and data minimization apply to storage, transport, and telemetry.

blocks.title: Sync efficiency controls
rows: Combine multiple commands into one request without changing their base revisions.
Reduces request overhead and saves battery.
Wait briefly before syncing rapid changes.
Avoids sending a request for every toggle.
Use idle time or app background events.
Keeps UI responsive and reduces contention.
Prevents one conflicting key from blocking the whole batch.
Lower bandwidth usage and faster sync.

blocks.title: Measured optimizations
items: Batch updates with a short debounce window.
Retry with exponential backoff and jitter.
Store the queue in IndexedDB for durability.
Use If-Match/ETag to avoid blind overwrites.
Expose a light sync indicator, not noisy toasts.

blocks.title: Synchronization failure and recovery
items: Conflict storms when multiple devices edit frequently.
Queue growth during long offline sessions.
Silent failures that leave the UI stuck in saving.

steps.title: 1. Device A offline changes
steps.text: User changes theme while offline; the command records the current theme base revision in the durable queue.

steps.title: 2. Device B online changes
steps.text: User changes theme again on another device; only the server revision for the theme key advances. An unrelated language or notifications update would not conflict with this command.

steps.title: 3. Device A reconnects
steps.text: SyncEngine sends the older theme command; its key-specific base revision is stale, so the server returns a conflict for theme only.

steps.title: 4. Merge and retry
steps.text: The client applies successful per-command outcomes, advances those key revisions, and retains only conflicting or retryable commands.

items.label: Primary metric
items.helperText: Measure how often commands apply on the first attempt.

items.label: Secondary metric
items.helperText: High conflict rate signals a merge strategy issue.

items.label: UX budget
items.helperText: The UI should never wait on the network.

blocks.title: Convergence invariant
blocks.text: Optimizing preference sync is about reliability and user trust. If you can show durable queues, smart retry, and conflict-aware merging, your design feels production-grade.

blocks.title: Failure modes
rows: Quarantine invalid records and keep confirmed preferences.
Ignore source and command identity already seen.
Reject the overlay and restore the confirmed value.
Use early validated bootstrap data and stable tokens.
The page avoids a persistent flash.

blocks.text: Preference controls use native labels, current values, and clear save or sync status. A remote change does not steal focus. Theme, contrast, motion, and text settings apply without removing visible focus or making controls unreachable. Conflicts explain the old and new values in text, not color alone.

Begin with one low-risk preference and same-tab persistence, then add tab and device sync. Observe queue age, conflicts, rollback, cross-tab loops, unauthorized writes, initial-theme flashes, and convergence time. Privacy-sensitive keys receive stricter review than cosmetic values.

blocks.title: cross device preferences sync answer rubric
items: Must — Track confirmed values and optimistic commands with a key-specific base revision.
Must — Persist offline commands and resolve conflicts only for the same key with a stale revision.
Strong signal — Apply independent per-key successes while retaining only conflicting or retryable commands.
Strong signal — Use a sync cursor and server revisions to converge tabs and devices deterministically.
Expert stretch — Explain preference-specific authority for privacy-sensitive settings and account changes.
Red flag — Treating an unrelated key update as a conflict or resolving all fields with one global timestamp.
